overview: The map’s Muscat label covers a broad Omani region from about 1000 to 1530, rather than one continuous kingdom ruled from the town. Inland Bahla and coastal Qalhat reveal different centres of power. Their archaeology helps explain the wider world of Muscat’s sailors, neighbours and trading partners.

periods.title: Omani ports and regional connections
periods.summary: Qalhat’s medieval trading history supplies regional context for the map’s early centuries; the imported starting year is not Muscat’s foundation.

periods.title: Inland rulers and maritime powers
periods.summary: Bahla was a Banu Nebhan centre, while Qalhat connected Oman to the Hormuzi trading world. These were distinct centres within the mapped region.

periods.title: Portuguese intervention
periods.summary: Portuguese power reached Muscat in 1507. The map stops this label in 1530, well before Portuguese rule ended there.

items.text: At inland Bahla, the Banu Nebhan made their capital and dominated central Oman from the twelfth to late fifteenth centuries. Their mud-brick fort stood on stone foundations beside an oasis. UNESCO places this political centre within Oman’s distinctive Ibadi Islamic setting.

Ibn Battuta described Muscat on his 1347 return journey as a small town with abundant fish. He placed this chain of Omani ports under Hormuz. His account catches one traveller’s particular moment, rather than defining five centuries of government.

Qalhat also had a woman in government: Bibi Maryam administered it during her husband Ayaz’s absences and continued after his death, remaining active at least until 1319. The great building associated with her name preserves a striking reminder of authority beyond kings alone.

sections.title: Ships, workshops and a connected coast

items.text: Qalhat, a separate port near present-day Sur, traded across the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean towards India and eastern Asia. Horses, dates, incense and pearls moved through its commercial networks. The coastline connected inland producers to customers far beyond Arabia.

An underwater survey in 1998 found more than twenty stone anchors off Qalhat. These heavy, practical objects give the vanished harbour a tangible presence: a busy trading port needed ways to stop its ships from drifting away.

Excavators uncovered a fourteenth-century pottery workshop at Qalhat. Chemical analysis helped separate locally made ceramics from imports. Some household containers therefore came from neighbourhood craftspeople, even in a port famous for distant connections.

Plant remains from workshop B39 include rice, finger millet, pulses and sesame. Researchers considered Indian and Yemeni connections, while leaving room for local cultivation. A seed can reveal a surprisingly international shopping list, but it does not carry its own shipping label.

sections.title: Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat

items.text: Building B94 contained two adjoining houses without an internal doorway between them. Courtyards organised domestic space, and some Qalhat houses probably had upper floors. Archaeology reveals neighbours and shared building patterns more securely than it reveals who was related to whom.

A study of B94 combined animal bones, fish remains and plant material. Their distribution suggested where food was processed and other household activities took place. The researchers treated these room functions as interpretations assembled from small traces left behind.

Among identified terrestrial animal remains at B94, sheep and goats dominated. Food also linked the port to date-palm gardens and livestock in its surrounding oasis economy. The dinner table depended on both maritime connections and nearby land.

Fish remains indicate intensive exploitation of open-water fishing grounds. Qalhat’s seafood supply was therefore connected to work beyond the beach: fishermen had to reach the waters where these fish lived before anyone could bring a catch home.

In workshop B39, plant material in room E suggested food preparation and crop cleaning. Craft and kitchen activities could leave traces in the same building. Researchers recovered familiar staples including dates, wheat and lentils alongside the less local crop possibilities.

sections.title: Water, bathing and finding tiny clues

items.text: Bahla’s oasis relied on wells and falaj channels that carried groundwater from distant sources. Keeping palms and people supplied required managing seasonal water as well. The surviving system illustrates the engineering and collective maintenance behind an apparently green patch in a dry landscape.

At Qalhat, a large vaulted cistern near Bibi Maryam’s monument held more than 280 cubic metres of water. Its roof reduced evaporation. Stone and waterproof sarooj mortar helped residents store a precious supply instead of letting the sun drink it first.

Qalhat’s partly excavated bathhouse had nine rooms, many with basins or tubs. Underground heating chambers, brick openings and pipes inside walls show how warmth circulated. Bathing here involved substantial plumbing and heating equipment, not simply carrying a bucket to the sea.

Modern archaeologists used sieving and flotation to recover tiny plant and animal remains from Qalhat’s buildings. In flotation, light material can be separated with water. These patient techniques make burnt seeds and other easily missed scraps useful evidence for ordinary life.

sections.title: A written glimpse and changing powers

items.text: A short Arabic witness is Ibn Battuta’s “فوصلت إلى مسقط”: “I arrived at Muscat.” This is a modern typeset transcription of his fourteenth-century travel account, not a local stone inscription or a surviving manuscript from the visit itself.

Qalhat’s decline is still being investigated. A geological study found displaced terrace deposits and altered stream courses along the Qalhat Fault, making earthquake activity a plausible contributor. This supports a possibility rather than a securely dated earthquake that explains everything.

Muscat’s harbour became a strategic Portuguese position after 1507. The occupation’s defensive system eventually included the paired forts Al Jalali and Al Mirani. Their later development must not be projected backwards onto every medieval scene shown by this map.

The later turning point came in 1650, when the Ya’aruba expelled the Portuguese from Muscat. This was part of a wider sequence of recoveries along the coast. Ports, residents and maritime skills continued through the change in political control.

ending.text: The imported label ends in 1530, but Muscat did not disappear then. Portuguese rule continued until 1650, followed by Omani control. The map boundary is a change of record, not the end of the town or its communities.
